scenario: Today's infrastructure track keeps circling two costs that grow fast. One is a KV cache that lengthens. The other is sparse or multimodal training that gets larger. On the training side, one stack is rebuilt for mixture-of-experts parallelism and precision, another cuts a multimodal pipeline by frozen state and attention work, and a fully open model fleet releases its data and intermediate checkpoints as well. On the serving side, 4-bit latent attention, the effect of evidence order on prefix caches in offline retrieval, memory-aligned cache packing, and snapshots for preempted requests are treated as one problem. An interruption or a recompute should not throw away work already done. The serving numbers on a new rack also show that split memory and 4-bit tensor cores do not turn into throughput by themselves. The kernels and the rack-wide cache have to change with them. Long video generation asks the same kind of question. How should a model keep a layered history of what it just wrote, so the picture can roll past the training horizon without collapsing?

papers.title: Supercharging Olmo-core for Efficient and Scalable MoE Training
papers.authors: Tianhua Tao, Akshita Bhagia, Dirk Groeneveld, Pete Walsh, Tyler Romero, Yashas Samaga, Jacob Morrison, Iz Beltagy, Taira Anderson, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models add parameters without proportionally increasing per-token compute. However, training cost also depends on bytes moved, memory held, and kernels launched, and many of those costs follow total parameter size rather than active compute. On infrastructure built for dense models, this mismatch is costly: in early baselines, throughput fell as stored expert parameter size grew, even though the useful work per token stayed nearly fixed. To close this gap, we present a redesigned training stack in Olmo-core, built for efficient, scalable MoE training. We replace the Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) of earlier Olmo-core versions with an architecture built on Distributed Data Parallel (DDP), and add Expert Parallelism (EP), Pipeline Parallelism (PP), a distributed optimizer, and activation recompute. We propose NVSHMEM-based rowwise EP, which writes each token directly into its expert's buffer, avoiding dispatch and combine permutation overhead. We make EP fully synchronization-free by keeping routing metadata on the GPU and using device-scheduled grouped GEMMs. Closely integrated MXFP8 cuts compute, activation-memory, and transport costs, and topology-agnostic checkpoints let the parallel layout change between runs. On NVL8 B300 nodes, the stack supports training configurations from 12.9 billion to 1.2 trillion total parameters on up to 512 GPUs, reaching 858 useful-model TFLOP/s/GPU at 1.2 trillion with MXFP8 and per-layer recompute; an experimental capacity test with the optional DeepEP v2 backend reaches 2.38 trillion. We also explain each design choice and share findings for other training systems; for example, we identify a failure pattern we call Token Gerrymandering, in which the MoE router can learn to hack the load-balancing loss, and find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides.
papers.summary: Mixture-of-experts models add parameters, but the useful compute per token barely changes. If the training stack still moves and stores parameters as a dense model would, throughput falls as the expert pool grows. Olmo-core replaces fully sharded data parallelism with distributed data parallelism, and adds expert parallelism, pipeline parallelism, a distributed optimizer, and activation rematerialization. On B300 eight-GPU nodes, with up to 512 GPUs, a 1.2-trillion-parameter run that uses MXFP8 (a microscaling 8-bit float format) and per-layer rematerialization reaches 858 useful-model TFLOPS per GPU per second. The authors also find that overlapping communication with computation can slow the overlapped kernels by more than it hides. ==Once experts multiply, the first bottleneck is moving parameters, not the math per step.== For teams training very large MoE models, parallelism, precision, and rematerialization have to be designed together, or useful compute is spent on traffic first.

papers.title: Efficient Distributed MLLM Training with Cornstarch
papers.authors: Insu Jang, Runyu Lu, Nikhil Bansal, Ang Chen, Mosharaf Chowdhury
papers.abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) extend the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by combining heterogeneous model architectures to handle diverse modalities like images and audio.
However, this inherent heterogeneity in MLLM model structure and data types makes makeshift extensions to existing LLM training frameworks unsuitable for efficient MLLM training, especially in distributed training.

In this paper, we present Cornstarch, an efficient distributed MLLM training framework that contemplates MLLM's unique characteristics in both model and data parallelization.
Cornstarch introduces frozen-aware pipeline parallelism and workload-balanced context parallelism to improve MLLM training throughput.
Our extensive evaluation shows that Cornstarch outperforms state-of-the-art solutions by $2.26\times$ on average in terms of MLLM training throughput.

Cornstarch is an open-source project and available on [Github](https://github.com/cornstarch-org/Cornstarch).
papers.summary: Multimodal models stitch vision or speech encoders together with a language model, so both the architecture and the data are uneven. Dropping them into a language-model training stack often leaves pipeline stages and context-parallel ranks badly balanced. When an encoder is frozen, a pipeline cut that assumed every module was trainable falls out of balance; tokens of different types also attend over different ranges,. Cornstarch splits the pipeline with frozen modules in mind, and assigns tokens in context parallelism by attention work. On 24 A40 GPUs, end-to-end training throughput rises to 2.26 times that of existing systems on average; after the frozen state is built into the cut, an iteration can be up to 2.46 times faster. ==The bottleneck in multimodal training is often idle time between unlike modules and unlike data.== For teams training vision-language models, the parallel cut has to see frozen weights and attention masks, rather than reuse a text-only plan.

papers.title: NVFP4-MLA: Unified FP4 KV-Cache Storage and Attention Computation for Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.authors: Chao Ni, Qi Zhang, Xiao Wang, Zongfei Jing, Mingyang Hao, Binghan Chen, Kefeng Duan, Yu-Jung Chen, Mengdi Wang, Tijmen Blankevoort, Jun Yang
papers.abstract: Long-context reasoning and agentic workloads make key-value (KV) cache capacity and attention computation the dominant costs of serving frontier large language models. We present NVFP4-MLA, the first design to push both KV-cache storage and attention computation of multi-head latent attention (MLA) to FP4. NVFP4-MLA co-designs the quantization algorithm with the attention kernel and the cache system. Selective residual compensation preserves model accuracy by adding NVFP4 residuals only to the quantization-sensitive channels. Two-dimensional quantization blocks make the shared latent cache compatible with the different reduction directions of the two attention batched matrix multiplications (BMMs), removing requantization between them. On DeepSeek-R1 and Kimi-K3, NVFP4-MLA matches BF16 MLA average accuracy across nine benchmarks while compressing the MLA KV cache by 3.20x and 3.05x relative to BF16 MLA. On NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, NVFP4-MLA speeds up the attention kernel over FP8 MLA by up to 2.82x on DeepSeek-R1 and 2.71x on Kimi-K3, and lowers p90 time to first token in agentic multi-turn serving by up to 3.5x and 2.1x, respectively. In disaggregated DeepSeek-R1 serving, it also raises per-GPU throughput by up to 2.30x.
papers.summary: In long-context reasoning and agent workloads, multi-head latent attention already shrinks the KV cache with a low-rank latent, but the cache still grows with length and concurrency, and attention compute can saturate first. Pushing both storage and attention to FP4 is not a drop-in change: sensitive channels need a residual, and one latent cache must serve the two reduction directions of the attention matrix multiplies. On DeepSeek-R1, the method compresses the MLA KV cache by 3.20 times relative to BF16, and speeds up the attention kernel by up to 2.82 times over FP8. In disaggregated serving, per-GPU throughput rises by up to 2.30 times, while average accuracy across nine benchmarks still matches BF16. ==To get the benefit of 4-bit MLA, storage, the kernel, and the cache layout have to change together.== For teams raising concurrency on long sessions, making this shared latent cache truly 4-bit in compute pays off more than compressing storage alone.

papers.title: KaleidoKV: Rearranging Evidence for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Offline RAG Inference
papers.authors: Peiting Xie, Xingyu Tan, Xiangjun Zai, Chen Chen, Xiaoyang Wang, Wenjie Zhang
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments large language models (LLMs) on question-answering (QA) tasks with retrieved evidence at inference time. Related questions in an offline batch often retrieve overlapping evidence, but prefix caching reuses key-value (KV) states only for identical token prefixes, making reuse dependent on evidence order. Although all questions and evidence are known before execution, existing reordering methods commit to early grouping decisions and can miss sharing opportunities that require several requests to move together. Evaluating alternative layouts can incur planning costs that offset inference savings, while concurrent requests may still recompute shared prefixes before their KV states become available. To address these challenges, we propose KaleidoKV, a framework that plans evidence orders across the batch and controls when requests enter the engine while preserving each request's evidence set and content. Joint layout planning revises formed groups through coordinated request moves and keeps a move only if it lowers planned prefill, the computation required when each shared prefix is computed once. A global prefix index selects evidence orders by locating reusable prefixes and evaluates each move incrementally from only the affected request paths. Prefix-ready admission tracks nested prefix dependencies, delaying requests whose shared prefixes are still being computed while allowing independent requests to proceed. Experiments on four QA workloads and four LLMs show that KaleidoKV achieves the highest throughput and lowest mean time to first token in all 16 settings, with approximately 1.24-1.75x the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. With Llama-3.1-8B under the default configuration, actual prefill stays within 0.5% of planned prefill across all four workloads.
papers.summary: In offline batch question answering, related questions often retrieve overlapping evidence, but a prefix cache can be reused only when the token prefixes match exactly, so a different evidence order forces a recompute. Existing reordering methods lock groups too early, and the planner itself can spend the prefill it hoped to save. KaleidoKV plans evidence order across the whole batch, keeps a move only when it lowers planned prefill, and admits dependent requests only after their shared prefixes are ready. In all sixteen settings it records the highest throughput and the lowest mean time to first token, at about 1.24 to 1.75 times the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. ==Evidence order is not a minor tweak; it decides whether the prefix cache can be shared at all.== For offline RAG batch inference, planning shared prefixes first and then controlling when requests enter the engine works better than tuning the cache one request at a time.

papers.title: K2-Horizon: A Frontier Fleet of Open Source Language Models
papers.authors: K2 Team, Zhengzhong Liu, Haonan Li, Xuezhe Ma, Alexander Moreno, Subham Sekhar Sahoo, Rupesh Kumar Srivastava, Mikhail Yurochkin, Hadi Abdine, Yash Akhauri, Adharsh Babu, David Bellamy, Jalaj Bhandari, Dani Bouch, Wail Bouhedja, Weili Cao, Ahmad Chamma, Po-Chun Chang, Junlin Chen, Lingjie Chen, Zhoujun Cheng, Kyle Chickering, Ryandito Diandaru, Evan Dufraisse, Chaitanya Dwivedi, Bilal El Bouardi, Desai Fan, Richard Fan, Chengqian Gao, Rifo Ahmad Genadi, Jonathan Geuter, Charles Guille-Escuret, Willis Guo, Dhawal Gupta, Seungwook Han, Tingxu Han, Shibo Hao, Besher Hassan, Guowei He, Ming Shan Hee, Joel Hestness, Yu Huang, Yuan Huang, Haolong Jia, Linghao Jin, Junu Kim, Lingjing Kong, Nurkhan Laiyk, Andrej Leban, Liqun Ma, John Maggs, Amr Mohamed, Mukhesh Narra, Omkar Pangarkar, Aldo Pareja, Khiem Pham, Varad Pimpalkhute, Nikhil Ranjan, Elizaveta Rebrova, Hector Ren, Shaurya Rohatgi, Guokan Shang, Jianshu She, Chufan Shi, Aaryamonvikram Singh, Daria Soboleva, Kartik Sreenivasan, Suqi Sun, Yuekai Sun, Bowen Tan, Liping Tang, Shengkun Tang, Muzi Tao, Mallikarjuna Tupakula, Micah Villmow, Hongyi Wang, Huijuan Wang, Renxi Wang, Yongxin Wang, Yuqi Wang, Zhenting Wang, Shicheng Wen, Yingquan Wu, Anze Xie, Andrew Xing, Matthew Yang, Shuanghai Yu, Kerem Zaman, Zenan Zhai, Hongli Zhan, Xuezhou Zhang, Anshun Asher Zheng, Zhe Zhou, Richard Zhuang, Eric P. Xing
papers.abstract: We present K2-Horizon, a fleet of six fully open language models, from a 0.9B dense model to a 375B-A23B MoE, built for general-purpose reasoning and agentic work across math and science, software engineering, deep research, office automation, and beyond. The models lead or are competitive with strong open models of their size on agentic and coding benchmarks. On the modeling side, to strengthen reasoning, we introduce Mixture-of-Value Attention (MoVA), applying MoE to attention value projections, and softplus attention gating, a more flexible, theoretically motivated gate. Our 36B-A4B model uses both and nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data, with one-seventh the active parameters. We also introduce Uno, lossless diffusion adapters that speed up decoding by up to 2.2x without a separate draft model. Our release follows the LLM360 definition of open source for transparency and reproducibility: the full development history, including intermediate checkpoints from every training stage, pre-training data, training logs, and all training, evaluation, and infrastructure code, notably our production-scale xLLM framework for dense and MoE training and the RL360 reinforcement-learning stack. Beyond the data itself, we release and document in detail every pipeline that built it, the part of model development that open releases most rarely disclose. These pipelines produced roughly 10T synthetic pre-training tokens, showing that synthetic data can be a major ingredient of pre-training at scale. Four of the models share one 22T-token pre-training corpus and recipe, revealing consistent scaling behavior and enabling controlled studies of scale and sparsity. All artifacts are available at https://ifm.ai/k2/
papers.summary: Open models that both match strong peers of the same size on reasoning and agent tasks, and also release their data, training process, and intermediate checkpoints, are still rare. K2-Horizon is a fully open fleet that runs from small dense models to a large mixture-of-experts model, and it also releases training logs and infrastructure code. Its 36B-A4B model uses mixture-of-value attention and, with about one-seventh the active parameters, nearly matches a 32B dense model trained on the same data. Uno, a lossless diffusion adapter, speeds up the 7B model by about 2.2 times at batch size 1, without a separate draft model. ==Open weights are not enough; the data and the training process need to be visible as well.== For anyone who wants to reproduce or continue training an open model, a dense and sparse pair trained on the same data and recipe is more useful than a final leaderboard score alone.

papers.title: MeltKV: Memory-Aligned KV Cache Compression via Variable-Bit Packed Vector Quantization for Long-Context LLMs
papers.authors: Jiyun Han, Seongjoon Cho, Seungkyu Choi
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on long contexts, making Key-Value (KV) caches dominate memory usage and inference latency. Existing vector quantization (VQ) methods effectively compress KV caches to sub-4-bit levels but often overlook inefficiencies in memory alignment and decoding speed. This work introduces MeltKV, a memory-latency co-optimized KV cache quantization framework for long-context LLM serving. MeltKV employs a memory-aligned variable-bit index packing scheme that adaptively assigns bit-widths to grouped key channels and compactly stores indices within standard data-types, eliminating redundant bits. Additionally, head-wise codebook sharing reduces the total codebook size while maintaining accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that MeltKV effectively compresses KV representations to sub-4-bit levels down to 1 bit and, at comparable perplexity, achieves 48.1% lower memory usage and 52.9% lower latency than state-of-the-art VQ methods.
papers.summary: In long-context inference, the KV cache quickly fills memory and slows decoding. Existing vector quantization can push the cache below 4 bits, but when indices are not packed into standard word widths and codebooks grow large, the saved space and speed disappear. Some methods share a global codebook to decode faster, then lose accuracy at lower bit-widths; others keep accuracy, but decode even slower than an uncompressed cache. MeltKV assigns variable bit widths to grouped key channels, packs the indices into standard data types, and shares a codebook across attention heads, dropping the padding that alignment would otherwise add. At comparable perplexity, it uses 48.05% less memory than the MILLION method and cuts decoding latency by 52.91% relative to CQ, a vector quantization method, and it can compress the representation down to 1 bit. ==Going to fewer bits is not enough; the indices have to be packed to match memory alignment.== For teams raising concurrency on long contexts, memory and decode latency have to be read together, not just the compression ratio.

papers.title: Making Preemption Productive in Long-Output LLM Serving
papers.authors: Ziji Shi, Xinyi Wan, Chaoyi Ruan, Guangxing Huang, Min Lin, Jialin Li
papers.abstract: Reasoning LLMs generate long outputs whose key--value (KV) caches occupy GPU memory for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request can repeatedly lose and recover its state while producing little new output. We call this behavior KV thrashing. In certain cases, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Because preemption cannot be avoided without delaying admission, we ask how to make it productive. We present Stint, a serving system that preserves a preempted request's work, bounds how long it waits, and gives it fresh output after it returns. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in a contiguity-first CPU pool with an exact-extent allocator, and moves them with fused K/V gather/scatter kernels and double buffering. Age-based readmission brings stalled requests back, and protection gives them a turn of fresh decoding before another preemption. Remaining-length estimates from decoding hidden states guide victim selection. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds under Stint and p99 time per output token falls by 50.7\% relative to recomputation in the same engine. The replay as a whole finishes 10.7\% sooner (12.0\% higher throughput), because the requests that baselines starve no longer finish last.
papers.summary: Reasoning models emit long outputs, and their KV caches can occupy a GPU for minutes. When memory fills, the server preempts requests, and a preempted request may repeatedly lose its state and then write few new tokens after it returns: cache thrashing. In the authors' replays, existing systems leave more than a fifth of requests stalled for over a minute. Stint stores fixed-length KV snapshots in CPU memory, readmits requests by how long they have waited, and guarantees a stretch of steady decoding after they return. On olympiad-math replays with Qwen3-32B on H200 GPUs, no request pauses for more than 50 seconds; P99 time per output token falls by 50.7% relative to recomputation in the same engine, and the replay finishes 10.7% sooner. ==Preemption cannot be avoided, but a preempted request should not lose the work it already did.== For serving long-output requests, keeping a snapshot and giving it an undisturbed decoding turn costs less than computing the same tokens again.

papers.title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.
papers.summary: In post-training quantization for large language models, GPTQ is the usual layer-wise solver, but it optimizes continuous group scales separately from discrete integer assignments, even though the two are coupled. JointQ, in group-wise quantization, recomputes a group's optimal scale in closed form whenever it changes one integer, and periodically re-solves all scales jointly. The search starts from candidates that include the GPTQ solution, so the unregularized layer-wise calibration error is never worse than GPTQ, and the weights stay in a format that can replace it directly. The gain in six-task average zero-shot accuracy grows from 0.0044 in a wide-group 4-bit setting to 0.1559 in 3-bit per-channel quantization, and the method beats vanilla GPTQ in fourteen of sixteen comparisons. ==At low bit-widths, scales and integers cannot be chosen by a greedy split.== For teams pushing models to 3-bit or to larger groups, fixing the solver itself may help more than preprocessing the weights alone.

papers.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s
papers.abstract: The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores
papers.summary: When DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash moves from a GB300 rack to a new Vera Rubin NVL72, kernels written for the older memory and math layout will not fill Rubin's split memory domains or its FP4 tensor cores. vLLM rebuilds the expert, attention, and communication paths for those two memory domains and wider matrix instructions, adds a specialized tensor-parallel decode path for the lowest latency, and uses a rack-wide KV cache plus routing to hold much higher concurrency. On the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark, one Rubin rack reaches 1.7 million tokens per second per GPU while each user still gets 387 tokens per second, which is 58 times the throughput of a GB300 NVL72. These figures come from rack-scale AgentX measurements, not a single-GPU microbenchmark. ==A new chip's throughput depends on whether the software was rewritten for its memory and instructions.== For teams serving models on a new rack, moving old kernels over is not enough; the shared cache and the router have to change with them.

papers.title: MovieRoll: A Systematic Framework for Rolling Out Long-Form Videos
papers.authors: Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian
papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.
papers.summary: Streaming long videos means quality has to hold past the training horizon, while the model also has to live with its own generated history and with a cache that keeps growing. MovieRoll first trains a multi-step base with window-wise teacher forcing, then compresses the historical KV cache by layer: shallow layers keep the full history, deeper layers keep only a sink and the recent tokens. Cache memory falls by up to 78%, and generation quality improves. After long-rollout distillation, the base model, trained on videos of up to 15 seconds, stays competitive at 30 seconds, and the distilled model records the highest total scores among the compared methods on longer single-event and multi-event evaluations. ==Long video generation has to manage the history the model just wrote, not merely train on longer clips.== For minute-scale video generation, layered caches and long self-rollout during training decide whether the picture can keep rolling without collapsing.
